# How to use this guide

Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety is a third-semester course of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum (2 credits theory, 40 hours; 1 credit practical, 40 hours of lab/experiential learning). It has two halves taught by different teachers but examined in **one 3-hour, 75-mark university paper**:

- **Section A: Applied Microbiology** — 20 hours, **37 marks**.
- **Section B: Infection Control and Safety** — 20 hours, **38 marks**.

Internal assessment adds 25 marks. You must pass theory with at least 50%. Because the two sections are written in one sitting, prepare both — a weak half pulls down the whole paper.

**How the units are arranged.** The INC syllabus has 4 units in Section A and 11 short units in Section B. To keep each notes file a useful size, units are split or joined as follows:

| Notes file | Section | INC unit(s) | Hours (theory) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Introduction and general characteristics of microbes | A | I + first half of II | 3 + about 5 |
| Unit 2 Staining, culture media and culture methods | A | Second half of II | about 5 |
| Unit 3 Pathogenic organisms, rodents and vectors | A | III | 4 |
| Unit 4 Immunity, hypersensitivity, serology and immunization | A | IV | 3 |
| Unit 5 HAI and bundles, isolation and PPE, hand hygiene | B | I + II + III | 2 + 3 + 1 |
| Unit 6 Disinfection and sterilization, specimen collection, BMW and laundry, antibiotic stewardship | B | IV + V + VI + VII | 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 |
| Unit 7 Patient safety indicators, incidents, IPSG | B | VIII + IX | 3 + 1 |
| Unit 8 Safety protocols and employee safety | B | X + XI | 2 + 2 |

Units 1–4 are Section A and Units 5–8 are Section B. Study one notes file a day; then answer that unit's questions and MCQs without looking.

**University paper pattern (75 marks, 3 hours)** — as given in INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3. There is no internal choice: every question must be answered. Your university may print it differently; confirm with your university.

| Section | MCQ | Essay (long) | Short | Very short | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A: Applied Microbiology | 6 × 1 = 6 | 1 × 10 = 10 | 3 × 5 = 15 | 3 × 2 = 6 | **37** |
| B: Infection Control including Safety | 7 × 1 = 7 | 1 × 10 = 10 | 3 × 5 = 15 | 3 × 2 = 6 | **38** |
| **Paper total** | 13 | 20 | 30 | 12 | **75** |

The mock test "University paper" follows this pattern. The app draws questions for each section from the whole question bank, so a Section A slot may sometimes show an infection-control question; in the real paper each section keeps to its own half. Use the unit filter to practise one section at a time.

Time plan for the real paper: MCQs 10 minutes, each essay about 30 minutes, each short answer 12–15 minutes, each very short answer 4–5 minutes, and 10 minutes to revise.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a favourite; comes up in most papers in some form. Learn the full answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and the usual style of B.Sc Nursing microbiology and infection control papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | History (Pasteur, Koch, Lister), chain of infection, bacterial cell structure, Gram-positive vs Gram-negative wall, spores, growth curve, factors affecting growth |
| 2 | Gram stain steps, ZN stain, culture media classification with examples, streak plate, anaerobic culture |
| 3 | *S. aureus*, *Streptococcus*, *M. tuberculosis*, *Salmonella* Typhi, *V. cholerae*, HIV and hepatitis B, classification of mycoses, malaria parasite, vectors and the diseases they spread |
| 4 | Types of immunity, immunoglobulin structure and classes, hypersensitivity types, Widal/VDRL/ELISA, types of vaccines, cold chain, National Immunization Schedule |
| 5 | HAI definition and the four bundles (CAUTI, SSI, VAP, CLABSI), standard and transmission-based precautions, donning and doffing PPE, 5 moments and steps of hand hygiene, infection control committee |
| 6 | Spaulding classification, autoclave and other sterilization methods, specimen collection (blood culture, urine, sputum), BMW colour coding, laundry, antibiotic stewardship, MRSA prevention |
| 7 | Incident reporting, RCA and CAPA, restraints, blood transfusion policy, fall prevention, WHO surgical safety checklist, IPSG |
| 8 | 5S, fire safety (classes, RACE, PASS), spill management, MSDS, emergency codes, nurse in disaster, needle-stick injury and PEP, hepatitis B vaccination of staff |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Start every essay with a definition**, then classification, then points with headings, then a **nursing role** section at the end. Examiners reward structure.
2. **Draw simple labelled diagrams**: bacterial cell, growth curve, streak plate, immunoglobulin, chain of infection, fishbone diagram, 5 moments. Pencil, straight label lines, a title.
3. Use **tables** for comparisons: Gram-positive vs Gram-negative, active vs passive immunity, IgG/IgA/IgM, contact vs droplet vs airborne precautions, sterilization vs disinfection, BMW colours.
4. For organisms, follow one order: **morphology → source and transmission → diseases → laboratory diagnosis → prevention → nursing care**.
5. Learn the numbers examiners like: autoclave 121 °C, 15 lb/in², 15–20 minutes; hot air oven 160 °C for 2 hours; hand rub 20–30 s, hand wash 40–60 s; head of bed 30–45°; cold chain 2–8 °C; untreated BMW not stored beyond 48 hours; HIV PEP within 72 hours (ideally 2), for 28 days; hepatitis B vaccine at 0, 1, 6 months.
6. Keep BMW colour coding exact (yellow, red, white translucent, blue) — it is asked almost every year as an essay, short answer or MCQ.
7. In Section B, answers are about **what the nurse does**. Write action points (verbs first: "check", "label", "report") rather than theory.
8. For very short answers (2 marks), give a one-line definition plus one example or one fact. Don't write a page.
9. MCQs come from small facts; read the "Remember" list of every notes file and the revision sheet the night before.

**Practical (lab/experiential) part**: the INC course includes 40 hours of lab and experiential learning — demonstrations of staining and culture, vaccine storage visits, hand hygiene and PPE re-demonstration, BMW and CSSD visits, mock drills. Practicals are assessed internally; this pack covers the theory paper.

# Unit 1: Introduction to microbiology and general characteristics of microbes

Section A (Applied Microbiology), INC Unit I (3 hours) joined with the first half of INC Unit II (structure, classification, morphology and growth of microbes). The laboratory half of Unit II — staining, media and culture — is in notes Unit 2.

## 1.1 What microbiology is and why a nurse needs it

**Microbiology** is the study of living things too small to be seen with the naked eye (micro-organisms or microbes): bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and the microscopic stages of worms (helminths). **Medical microbiology** deals with those that live on or in humans and cause disease.

Microbes are everywhere — in soil, water, air, on skin, in the gut. Most are harmless or useful (gut flora that make vitamin K, bacteria used to make curd and vaccines). Only a small number are **pathogens**.

**Importance and relevance to nursing**

| Area of nursing work | How microbiology helps |
| --- | --- |
| Infection prevention | Knowing how microbes spread lets the nurse break the chain of infection: hand hygiene, asepsis, isolation, sterilization |
| Specimen collection | Correct sample, correct time, correct container and quick transport give a correct report |
| Patient care | Recognising signs of infection (fever, pus, raised pulse), wound care, catheter and line care |
| Medicines | Giving antibiotics on time, after cultures are sent, and supporting antibiotic stewardship |
| Immunization | Storing vaccines in the cold chain, giving them correctly, recognising adverse events |
| Community health | Safe water, food hygiene, vector control, outbreak reporting |
| Own safety | Needle-stick prevention, staff vaccination, safe handling of specimens and waste |

## 1.2 Historical perspective

| Scientist | Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (17th century, Netherlands) | Made simple microscopes and first described microbes ("animalcules"); called the father of microbiology (and of bacteriology) |
| Edward Jenner (1796) | Protected people against smallpox using cowpox material — the beginning of vaccination |
| Ignaz Semmelweis (1840s, Vienna) | Showed that hand washing by doctors in chlorinated lime solution cut deaths from puerperal (childbed) fever |
| Florence Nightingale (1850s) | Cut deaths in military hospitals through cleanliness, ventilation, nutrition and records; founder of modern nursing |
| Louis Pasteur (France) | Disproved spontaneous generation; germ theory of disease; pasteurization; vaccines against anthrax, chicken cholera and rabies; father of modern microbiology |
| Joseph Lister (1867) | Antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid (phenol); father of antiseptic surgery |
| Robert Koch (Germany) | Isolated the causes of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera; solid media and pure culture methods; Koch's postulates |
| Hans Christian Gram (1884) | Gram staining |
| Dmitri Ivanovsky, Martinus Beijerinck (1890s) | Discovered filterable agents — the first viruses (tobacco mosaic virus) |
| Paul Ehrlich | Idea of the "magic bullet" — a drug that kills microbes but spares the host |
| Alexander Fleming (1928) | Discovered penicillin |

**Koch's postulates** (to prove an organism causes a disease):

1. The organism is found in every case of the disease.
2. It can be isolated and grown in pure culture.
3. The pure culture causes the same disease when put into a susceptible animal.
4. The same organism can be recovered again from that animal.

Exceptions exist: some organisms cannot be grown in culture (*Mycobacterium leprae*, *Treponema pallidum*), and carriers may have the organism without disease.

## 1.3 Concepts and terminology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Pathogen | An organism that can cause disease |
| Opportunistic pathogen | Normally harmless, causes disease when defences are low (e.g. *Candida* in diabetes, *Pneumocystis* in AIDS) |
| Commensal / normal flora | Organisms that live on the body without harm and often protect it by competing with pathogens |
| Pathogenicity | Ability to cause disease |
| Virulence | Degree of pathogenicity — how severe the disease is |
| Infection | Entry and multiplication of a pathogen in the body |
| Contamination | Presence of microbes on a surface or object |
| Colonisation | Organisms grow on a body site without causing illness |
| Carrier | A person who harbours a pathogen without symptoms and can pass it on (e.g. typhoid carrier) |
| Reservoir | Where the organism normally lives and multiplies (human, animal, soil, water) |
| Incubation period | Time from entry of the organism to the first symptom |
| Endogenous infection | From the patient's own flora |
| Exogenous infection | From outside — other people, equipment, environment |
| Nosocomial / healthcare-associated infection | Acquired in a healthcare setting; not present or incubating at admission |
| Zoonosis | Disease spread from animals to humans (rabies, plague, leptospirosis) |
| Toxin | Poisonous product: **exotoxin** (protein released by living bacteria, e.g. tetanus, diphtheria toxin) or **endotoxin** (lipopolysaccharide of the Gram-negative cell wall, released when cells die; causes fever and shock) |
| Asepsis | Absence of pathogens; aseptic technique keeps them away |
| Sterilization | Killing or removing all microbes, including spores |
| Disinfection | Killing most harmful microbes on objects, usually not spores |
| Antiseptic | A chemical that can be safely used on living tissue to kill or inhibit microbes |

## 1.4 Principles of microbiology

1. Microbes are everywhere; most are harmless or useful.
2. Each disease has a specific cause (germ theory).
3. Microbes need food, water, the right temperature, pH and oxygen conditions to grow. Remove these and they stop growing.
4. Microbes spread by definite routes — the **chain of infection** — and each link can be broken.
5. They can be killed or removed by physical and chemical agents (sterilization, disinfection).
6. The body defends itself through natural and acquired immunity; vaccines build acquired immunity.
7. Microbes change: they can become resistant to antibiotics.

**Chain of infection**

```text
 Infectious agent → Reservoir → Portal of exit → Mode of transmission
        ↑                                                   ↓
 Susceptible host ←──────────── Portal of entry ←───────────┘
```

| Link | Examples | How the nurse breaks it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent | Bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites | Early diagnosis, treatment, disinfection |
| Reservoir | Patients, carriers, staff, water, equipment | Cleaning, isolation, staff health checks |
| Portal of exit | Respiratory secretions, blood, urine, faeces, wound pus | Cover coughs, dressings, safe disposal of body fluids |
| Mode of transmission | Contact (direct, indirect), droplet, airborne, vehicle (food, water, blood), vector | Hand hygiene, PPE, sterilization, isolation, vector control |
| Portal of entry | Broken skin, mucosa, urinary catheter, IV line, ventilator tube | Aseptic technique, catheter and line care |
| Susceptible host | Newborns, elderly, diabetics, cancer patients, ICU patients | Immunization, nutrition, skin care |

## 1.5 Classification of microbes

All living things are grouped into cells with a true nucleus (**eukaryotes**) and cells without (**prokaryotes**). Viruses are not cells at all.

| Feature | Prokaryote (bacteria) | Eukaryote (fungi, protozoa, human cells) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nucleus | No nuclear membrane; single circular chromosome in the nucleoid | True nucleus with membrane; several chromosomes |
| Organelles | No mitochondria, no endoplasmic reticulum | Mitochondria, ER, Golgi body |
| Ribosomes | 70S | 80S |
| Cell wall | Peptidoglycan (except mycoplasma) | Fungi: chitin; protozoa and animal cells: none |
| Division | Binary fission | Mitosis |
| Size | Usually 1–10 µm | Usually 10–100 µm |

**Groups of medically important microbes**

| Group | Features | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bacteria | Single-celled prokaryotes; cell wall; divide by binary fission | *Staphylococcus*, *E. coli*, *Mycobacterium* |
| Viruses | Not cells; DNA or RNA in a protein coat; grow only inside living cells | HIV, hepatitis B, influenza, dengue |
| Fungi | Eukaryotes; yeasts (single cells) and moulds (threads called hyphae) | *Candida*, *Aspergillus*, dermatophytes |
| Protozoa | Single-celled animal-like eukaryotes | *Plasmodium*, *Entamoeba*, *Giardia* |
| Helminths | Multicellular worms; eggs and larvae are microscopic | Roundworm, hookworm, tapeworm |
| Special bacteria | Rickettsiae and chlamydiae (live inside cells), mycoplasma (no cell wall), spirochaetes (spiral, flexible) | Scrub typhus agent, *Chlamydia trachomatis*, *Treponema pallidum* |

Bacteria are also classified by **shape**, **Gram staining**, **oxygen need**, and **spore formation**.

## 1.6 Structure of a bacterial cell

```text
          flagellum
             ~~~~~
   ┌──────────────────────────┐ ← capsule (slime layer outside)
   │ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ ← cell wall (peptidoglycan)
   │ │ ┌──────────────────┐ │ │ ← cytoplasmic membrane
   │ │ │  nucleoid (DNA)  │ │ │
   │ │ │  ribosomes  ○ ○  │ │ │
   │ │ │  plasmid ◯       │ │ │
   │ │ └──────────────────┘ │ │
   │ └──────────────────────┘ │
   └──────────────────────────┘
       | | | |  pili / fimbriae
```

| Part | Structure | Importance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capsule | Layer of polysaccharide (sometimes polypeptide) outside the wall | Resists phagocytosis → more virulent (pneumococcus, *Klebsiella*); seen by negative staining; used in vaccines (pneumococcal, Hib) |
| Cell wall | Rigid peptidoglycan layer that gives shape | Basis of Gram staining; target of penicillins; Gram-negative wall carries endotoxin |
| Cytoplasmic membrane | Lipid bilayer | Controls entry and exit; site of energy production |
| Cytoplasm | Contains ribosomes (70S), granules (e.g. volutin granules of diphtheria bacilli) | Ribosomes are the target of several antibiotics |
| Nucleoid | Single circular DNA, no nuclear membrane | Carries genes |
| Plasmids | Small extra pieces of circular DNA | Often carry antibiotic-resistance genes; pass between bacteria |
| Flagella | Long whip-like threads | Movement (motility) |
| Pili (fimbriae) | Short hair-like threads | Attachment to host cells (e.g. *E. coli* to the bladder lining); sex pili transfer DNA |
| Spores (endospores) | Resting form with a thick coat, formed inside the cell in bad conditions | Resist heat, drying and disinfectants; *Bacillus* and *Clostridium*; killed only by sterilization |

**Gram-positive versus Gram-negative cell wall**

| Feature | Gram-positive | Gram-negative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Peptidoglycan | Thick, many layers | Thin, one or two layers |
| Teichoic acid | Present | Absent |
| Outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide | Absent | Present (endotoxin) |
| Colour in Gram stain | Purple / violet | Pink / red |
| Examples | *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, *Clostridium* | *E. coli*, *Salmonella*, *Pseudomonas*, *Neisseria* |

Acid-fast bacteria (*Mycobacterium*) have a waxy wall rich in mycolic acid, so they need the Ziehl–Neelsen stain.

## 1.7 Morphological types, size and form

Bacteria are measured in micrometres (µm; 1 µm = 1/1000 mm). Most cocci are about 1 µm across; most bacilli are 1–5 µm long. They are seen with the light microscope (oil immersion lens, ×100 objective). Viruses are much smaller (about 20–300 nm) and need the electron microscope.

```text
 COCCI (round)                 BACILLI (rods)        OTHERS
 ●●           diplococci       ▬                    ⌒  vibrio (comma)
 ●●●●●●       streptococci     ▬▬  diplobacilli     ∿∿ spirilla (rigid spiral)
 ●●●          staphylococci    ▬▬▬ streptobacilli   ∿∿∿∿ spirochaetes (flexible)
 ●●●            (grape-like    ▭  coccobacilli
  ●●             clusters)     branching threads — actinomycetes
 ●● tetrads, ●●●● cubes of 8 — sarcina
```

| Shape | Arrangement | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cocci | Pairs (diplococci) | Pneumococcus (lancet-shaped), *Neisseria* (kidney-shaped) |
| | Chains | *Streptococcus* |
| | Grape-like clusters | *Staphylococcus* |
| Bacilli | Single rods | *E. coli*, *Salmonella* |
| | Chinese-letter pattern | *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* |
| Comma-shaped | — | *Vibrio cholerae* |
| Spiral | Rigid / flexible | *Spirillum* / *Treponema*, *Leptospira* |
| No fixed shape (no cell wall) | — | *Mycoplasma* |

## 1.8 Motility

Most motile bacteria move by flagella.

| Arrangement of flagella | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Monotrichous — one flagellum at one end | *Vibrio cholerae* (darting motility) |
| Lophotrichous — a tuft at one end | *Spirillum* |
| Amphitrichous — at both ends | some spirilla |
| Peritrichous — all around the cell | *E. coli*, *Salmonella*, *Proteus* (swarming) |
| Atrichous — no flagella (non-motile) | *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, *Klebsiella*, *Shigella* |

Spirochaetes move by internal axial filaments. Motility is tested by the **hanging drop** method or in semi-solid agar.

## 1.9 Colonisation

Colonisation means organisms settling and growing on a body surface. Steps in infection: **attachment** (by pili, capsule) → **colonisation** (multiplying on the surface) → **invasion** (entering tissues using enzymes such as hyaluronidase, coagulase) → **damage** (by toxins or the body's own inflammatory reaction).

Normal flora colonise the skin (*Staphylococcus epidermidis*), mouth and throat (viridans streptococci), large intestine (*E. coli*, *Bacteroides*) and vagina (lactobacilli, which keep the pH acid). They protect by using up nutrients and space (colonisation resistance). Antibiotics that kill normal flora allow overgrowth of *Candida* or *Clostridioides difficile*.

In hospitals, patients' skin, nose and gut quickly become colonised with resistant hospital organisms (MRSA, resistant Gram-negative bacilli). Colonised patients are a reservoir even when they are not ill — the reason for hand hygiene between every patient.

## 1.10 Growth and nutrition of microbes

Bacteria multiply by **binary fission** — one cell splits into two. The time taken to double is the **generation time** (about 20 minutes for *E. coli* in good conditions; about 14–15 hours for *M. tuberculosis*, which is why TB cultures take weeks).

**Bacterial growth curve** (in a closed liquid culture)

```text
 log number
 of cells
   │            ┌────────────┐ stationary
   │           /              \
   │          /  log           \ decline
   │         /  (exponential)   \ (death)
   │  ______/                    \
   │  lag                         \
   └──────────────────────────────────→ time
```

1. **Lag phase** — cells adjust, make enzymes; no increase in number.
2. **Log (exponential) phase** — fastest division; cells most sensitive to antibiotics.
3. **Stationary phase** — food runs out, waste builds up; births = deaths; spores and exotoxins often formed.
4. **Decline (death) phase** — cells die faster than they divide.

**Nutrition**: bacteria need water, a carbon source, nitrogen, minerals and sometimes growth factors (vitamins, blood). Most pathogens are **heterotrophs** (use organic carbon from other living things). Fastidious organisms need enriched media (blood, serum).

**Factors that affect growth**

| Factor | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Temperature | **Psychrophiles** grow best in the cold (below 20 °C); **mesophiles** at 25–40 °C — all human pathogens, optimum about 37 °C; **thermophiles** at 55–80 °C. Refrigeration slows growth; heat kills |
| Moisture | Water is essential; drying stops growth (dried foods keep). Spores and some bacteria (*M. tuberculosis*, *Staphylococcus*) survive drying in dust |
| Oxygen | **Obligate aerobes** need O2 (*Pseudomonas*, *M. tuberculosis*); **facultative anaerobes** grow with or without (*E. coli*, *Staphylococcus*); **microaerophiles** need a little (*Campylobacter*, *Helicobacter*); **obligate anaerobes** are killed by O2 (*Clostridium*, *Bacteroides*) |
| Carbon dioxide | Some (*Neisseria*, *Brucella*) grow better in 5–10% CO2 (candle jar) |
| pH | Most pathogens prefer pH 7.2–7.6; *Vibrio cholerae* grows in alkaline pH; lactobacilli and fungi tolerate acid |
| Light | Ultraviolet rays and direct sunlight kill many bacteria |
| Osmotic pressure | High salt or sugar draws water out of cells (pickles, jam); *Staphylococcus aureus* tolerates salt |
| Blood and body fluids | Blood, serum, urine, pus and tissue fluid are rich in nutrients and keep organisms alive and growing — the reason spills of blood and body fluids are treated as infectious, and why stagnant urine in a catheter bag lets bacteria multiply |

## 1.11 Application and implication in nursing

- **Temperature**: specimens for culture are sent promptly; urine may be refrigerated (2–8 °C) if delayed so bacteria do not multiply and give a falsely high count. CSF and blood cultures are never refrigerated, because the organisms that cause meningitis die in the cold.
- **Moisture**: wet dressings and damp linen favour growth — keep wounds and skin folds dry; dry equipment fully after cleaning.
- **Oxygen**: deep, dirty wounds with dead tissue are anaerobic — risk of tetanus and gas gangrene; good wound debridement and immunization protect.
- **Spores** survive boiling and most disinfectants, so surgical instruments must be sterilized, not merely disinfected.
- **Normal flora**: unnecessary antibiotics upset the flora — watch for oral thrush and diarrhoea.
- **Body fluids**: treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious (standard precautions).
- Understand that the log phase is when infection spreads fastest — give antibiotics on time and do not miss doses.

## Remember

- Leeuwenhoek — first saw microbes; Pasteur — germ theory, rabies vaccine; Koch — TB bacillus, postulates; Lister — antiseptic surgery; Jenner — smallpox vaccine; Semmelweis — hand washing; Fleming — penicillin.
- Chain of infection has six links: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
- Prokaryotes: no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, binary fission. Viruses are not cells and grow only inside living cells.
- Gram-positive = thick peptidoglycan, purple. Gram-negative = thin wall + outer membrane with endotoxin, pink.
- Spores (*Bacillus*, *Clostridium*) are the most resistant forms; only sterilization kills them.
- Capsule resists phagocytosis; pili help attachment; flagella give motility; plasmids carry resistance genes.
- Growth curve: lag → log → stationary → decline.
- Human pathogens are mesophiles, optimum 37 °C.
- Obligate anaerobes: *Clostridium*, *Bacteroides*.

# Unit 2: Laboratory identification: staining, culture media and culture methods

Section A (Applied Microbiology), second half of INC Unit II: laboratory methods for identifying micro-organisms — staining, culture media, pure culture techniques and anaerobic culture. The nurse does not usually run these tests, but must understand them to collect the right specimen and to read a report.

## 2.1 How a microbiology laboratory identifies an organism

```text
Specimen received → Direct examination (wet mount, stained smear)
                  → Culture on suitable media (18–48 hours; weeks for TB)
                  → Identification (colony appearance, Gram stain of colony,
                    biochemical tests, automated systems)
                  → Antibiotic sensitivity testing
                  → Serology / antigen tests / molecular tests (PCR) where needed
                  → Report to the ward
```

**Direct microscopy** gives a quick first answer (Gram-positive cocci in clusters, acid-fast bacilli seen) within an hour; culture confirms the species and its antibiotic sensitivity.

**Wet preparations** (unstained):

- **Saline wet mount** — motile protozoa (trophozoites of *Entamoeba*, *Trichomonas*), pus cells.
- **Iodine mount** — cysts of protozoa in stool.
- **Hanging drop** — motility of bacteria (darting motility of *Vibrio cholerae*).
- **KOH mount** — fungi in skin, hair and nail (see 2.4).

## 2.2 Staining: principles

Bacteria are almost transparent, so they are stained to be seen. A smear is made on a clean glass slide, **air-dried** and **heat-fixed** (passed quickly through a flame two or three times) so the cells stick to the slide and are killed.

| Type | Principle | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple stain | One basic dye stains all cells the same colour; shows shape and arrangement | Methylene blue, crystal violet, dilute carbol fuchsin |
| Differential stain | Two dyes separate bacteria into groups | Gram stain, Ziehl–Neelsen (acid-fast) stain |
| Special stain | Shows a particular structure | Capsule (negative staining), spore stain, Albert's stain for metachromatic granules |
| Fungal preparations | Show fungal elements | Lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB), KOH mount |

## 2.3 Differential stains

### Gram stain

| Step | Reagent | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Primary stain | Crystal violet, about 1 minute | All cells stain purple |
| 2. Mordant | Gram's iodine, about 1 minute | Forms a crystal violet–iodine complex that is held firmly in thick walls |
| 3. Decolouriser | Acetone or alcohol, a few seconds, then wash | Removes the dye from Gram-negative cells (thin wall, outer membrane dissolved) |
| 4. Counterstain | Safranin (or dilute carbol fuchsin), about 30 seconds to 1 minute | Stains decolourised cells pink |

Result: **Gram-positive** = purple/violet; **Gram-negative** = pink/red.

```text
 Gram +ve:  thick peptidoglycan traps dye–iodine complex → stays PURPLE
 Gram −ve:  thin wall + outer membrane, decolourised → takes safranin → PINK
```

Uses: first clue to the cause of infection (e.g. Gram-negative diplococci inside pus cells in urethral pus suggest gonorrhoea; Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest staphylococci), and to guide early antibiotic choice.

### Ziehl–Neelsen (acid-fast bacilli, AFB) stain

Mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acid in the wall; they resist ordinary stains but, once stained with hot carbol fuchsin, they resist decolourisation by acid — hence "acid-fast".

| Step | Reagent | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Primary stain | Strong carbol fuchsin, heated until steam rises (do not boil) for about 5 minutes | Heat drives the dye through the waxy wall |
| 2. Decolouriser | 20% sulphuric acid (5% for *M. leprae*), then acid–alcohol in some methods | Removes dye from non-acid-fast cells |
| 3. Counterstain | Methylene blue (or malachite green) | Background and other cells stain blue |

Result: **acid-fast bacilli = bright red/pink rods** on a blue background. Used for sputum in tuberculosis (national programme sputum microscopy) and slit-skin smears in leprosy. Fluorescent staining (auramine) is a faster, more sensitive alternative used in larger laboratories.

## 2.4 Special stains and fungal preparations

| Stain | How it works | Result / use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Capsule — negative staining** (India ink or nigrosin) | The dark background stains, but the capsule does not take the dye | Clear halo around the organism against a black background; used for *Cryptococcus neoformans* in CSF; capsules of pneumococcus, *Klebsiella* |
| **Spore stain** (e.g. malachite green with heat, counterstain safranin) | Heat drives green dye into the tough spore coat | Green spores inside pink cells; *Bacillus*, *Clostridium* |
| **Albert's stain** | Toluidine blue and malachite green | Bluish-black metachromatic (volutin) granules in green bacilli — *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* |
| **LPCB (lactophenol cotton blue)** | Phenol kills fungi, lactic acid preserves structure, cotton blue stains chitin | Blue fungal hyphae and spores; used to identify moulds grown in culture |
| **KOH mount** (10–20% potassium hydroxide) | KOH dissolves keratin of skin, hair and nail, leaving fungi intact | Branching hyphae or spores seen directly; used for ringworm (dermatophytes), candidiasis of skin and nails |

Nursing points for KOH samples: scrape the active edge of a skin lesion with a sterile blade onto black paper or into a clean envelope; clip nails or pluck hair; do not apply creams before sampling.

## 2.5 Culture media

A **culture medium** is a preparation of nutrients on or in which microbes are grown in the laboratory. Bacteria grow as visible **colonies** on solid media and as turbidity (cloudiness) in liquid media.

**Ingredients**: water; peptone (protein digest — nitrogen); meat extract or yeast extract (vitamins, minerals); sodium chloride; **agar** (a seaweed polysaccharide used to solidify — it melts at about 100 °C and sets at about 40 °C and is not digested by most bacteria); and special additives (blood, serum, sugars, indicators, inhibitors).

**Media preparation (outline)**: weigh ingredients → dissolve in distilled water → adjust pH (about 7.2–7.4) → add agar for solid media → dispense into tubes or flasks → sterilize by autoclaving (heat-sensitive additives such as blood or serum are added after cooling to about 50 °C) → pour into Petri dishes or set as slopes → check sterility by incubating a sample → label and store in the refrigerator.

### Classification by physical state

| Type | Agar | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid | About 1.5–2% | Colonies, pure culture, colony counts (plates, slopes) |
| Semi-solid | About 0.2–0.5% | Motility testing, transport |
| Liquid (broth) | None | Growing large numbers, blood culture bottles, enrichment |

### Classification by composition

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synthetic (chemically defined) | Every ingredient and its amount known | Used in research and nutrition studies |
| Semi-synthetic | Mostly defined ingredients plus a small amount of a natural substance of unknown composition | A defined salts-and-sugar medium with added yeast extract |
| Complex / non-synthetic | Contains natural extracts (peptone, meat extract, blood) of variable composition | Nutrient agar, blood agar (most routine media) |

### Classification by purpose

| Type | Principle | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basal / simple | Supports organisms that are not fastidious | Nutrient broth, nutrient agar, peptone water |
| **Enriched** | Basal medium plus blood, serum or egg to grow fastidious organisms | Blood agar (5–10% sheep blood), chocolate agar (heated blood — *Haemophilus*, *Neisseria*), Loeffler's serum slope (diphtheria) |
| **Enrichment** (liquid) | Liquid that favours the wanted organism and holds back others, so a few pathogens in a mixed specimen can multiply before plating | Selenite F broth and tetrathionate broth (*Salmonella*, *Shigella* in stool), alkaline peptone water (*Vibrio cholerae*) |
| **Selective** (solid) | Contains substances that allow only the wanted organism to grow | Lowenstein–Jensen medium (*M. tuberculosis*; malachite green inhibits others), TCBS agar (*Vibrio*), deoxycholate citrate agar and XLD (*Salmonella*, *Shigella*), Sabouraud's agar with antibiotics (fungi) |
| **Differential** (indicator) | Colonies of different organisms look different | **MacConkey agar** — lactose fermenters (*E. coli*, *Klebsiella*) give pink colonies, non-fermenters (*Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Pseudomonas*) pale; **blood agar** shows haemolysis (alpha — green, beta — clear zone, gamma — none) |
| Transport | Keeps organisms alive without letting them multiply, during transport | Stuart's and Amies media (swabs), Cary–Blair (stool), viral transport medium (VTM) |
| Anaerobic | Contain reducing agents that remove oxygen | Robertson's cooked meat broth, thioglycollate broth |

Many media are both selective and differential (MacConkey agar contains bile salts that stop most Gram-positive bacteria and lactose with an indicator to show fermentation).

## 2.6 Pure culture techniques

A **pure culture** contains only one kind of organism, grown from a single colony. Clinical specimens are mixed, so the laboratory separates organisms first.

| Method | How it is done | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Streak plate** | A loop of specimen is spread over one area of an agar plate, then streaked in successive areas, flaming the loop between them, so organisms are thinned out and single colonies form in the last areas | Routine method for isolating pathogens |
| **Pour plate** | A measured amount of diluted specimen is mixed with melted, cooled (about 45 °C) agar and poured into a Petri dish; colonies grow throughout and on the surface | Counting viable bacteria (water, milk) |
| **Spread plate** | A small measured volume of diluted specimen is spread evenly over the surface with a sterile bent glass rod (L-shaped spreader) | Counting colonies; isolation |
| **Tube (serial) dilution** | The specimen is diluted step by step (1 in 10, 1 in 100, …) in tubes of sterile broth or saline; dilutions are then plated | Estimating numbers of organisms; also used to find the lowest concentration of an antibiotic that stops growth (MIC) |

```text
 Streak plate (four-quadrant method)
   ┌───────────────┐
   │ 1 ≡≡≡≡        │   1 = heavy growth (inoculum)
   │      2 ////   │   2, 3 = thinner
   │  4 ··  3 \\\\ │   4 = separate (isolated) colonies
   └───────────────┘
```

Plates are incubated upside down (lid down) at 37 °C so condensation does not drip on the colonies.

**Colony count in urine**: a calibrated loop places a known volume on the plate; counts of 10^5 (100,000) colony-forming units per mL or more in a properly collected midstream specimen usually mean significant urinary infection.

## 2.7 Anaerobic cultivation of bacteria

Obligate anaerobes (*Clostridium*, *Bacteroides*) die in oxygen, so they need special methods:

1. **Reducing media** — Robertson's cooked meat broth (meat particles contain reducing substances), thioglycollate broth.
2. **McIntosh–Fildes anaerobic jar** — plates are placed in a sealed metal or plastic jar; oxygen is removed by a catalyst that combines it with hydrogen to form water. Modern jars use a **gas-generating sachet (GasPak)**, which releases hydrogen and carbon dioxide when water is added. An indicator (methylene blue strip) turns colourless when the jar is anaerobic.
3. **Anaerobic chambers / workstations** — sealed cabinets filled with an oxygen-free gas mixture.
4. Older methods: boiling media to drive off oxygen, sealing with paraffin, candle jar (this only raises CO2 and is for capnophiles, not true anaerobes).

Specimens for anaerobic culture: pus aspirated in a syringe (better than a swab), tissue pieces; sent quickly in anaerobic transport medium; never refrigerated.

## 2.8 Other identification and sensitivity tests (overview)

| Test | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Biochemical tests (catalase, coagulase, oxidase, sugar fermentation, indole, urease) | Identify species (e.g. coagulase-positive = *S. aureus*) |
| Antibiotic sensitivity testing (Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion; MIC methods) | Reports organisms as sensitive, intermediate or resistant to each antibiotic |
| Automated systems (blood culture machines, identification and sensitivity analysers) | Faster results |
| Serology (ELISA, agglutination) | Detects antibodies or antigens (see Unit 4) |
| Molecular tests (PCR, cartridge-based nucleic acid tests for TB) | Detect DNA/RNA; fast and sensitive; also detect drug resistance genes |
| Animal inoculation and tissue culture | Mostly for research and virus isolation |

## 2.9 Application and implication in nursing

- Send specimens **before starting antibiotics**; antibiotics already given may stop organisms growing and give a falsely negative culture.
- Use the **correct container and transport medium** (VTM for viral swabs, Cary–Blair for stool if delayed, blood culture bottles for blood).
- Label specimens with patient details, specimen type, site, date and time, and any antibiotics given.
- A **Gram stain report** comes first and may change treatment within hours; tell the doctor promptly. The **culture and sensitivity** report comes in 2–3 days (weeks for TB culture).
- In TB, collect good-quality sputum (deep cough, not saliva) for AFB smear and molecular testing as directed by the national TB programme.
- Know that "no growth" from a poorly collected or delayed specimen does not rule out infection.
- Handle all specimens and cultures as infectious; laboratory staff are protected only if containers are leak-proof and correctly packed.

## Remember

- Gram stain order: crystal violet → iodine (mordant) → acetone/alcohol (decolouriser) → safranin (counterstain). Positive purple, negative pink.
- ZN stain: hot carbol fuchsin → 20% H2SO4 → methylene blue; AFB stain red.
- Negative staining (India ink) shows capsule of *Cryptococcus*; Albert's stain shows granules of *C. diphtheriae*; LPCB for fungal culture; KOH for skin, hair, nail.
- Enriched = blood/chocolate agar; enrichment = liquid (selenite F, alkaline peptone water); selective = LJ, TCBS; differential = MacConkey (pink lactose fermenters), blood agar (haemolysis).
- Pure culture: streak (routine), pour and spread (counts), tube dilution (counts, MIC).
- Anaerobes: Robertson's cooked meat medium, McIntosh–Fildes jar with GasPak.
- Specimens before antibiotics; correct container; quick transport.

# Unit 3: Pathogenic organisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, rodents and vectors

Section A (Applied Microbiology), INC Unit III. For each group: characteristics, source, portal of entry, transmission and how the organism is identified. Learn the tables — short answers and MCQs come straight from them.

## 3.1 How pathogens cause disease (overview)

| Step | What happens | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry | Through respiratory tract, gut, skin breaks, genital tract, blood, placenta | Droplets, food, needle, sexual contact |
| Attachment and colonisation | Pili, capsule, adhesins | *E. coli* in the urinary tract |
| Invasion and spread | Enzymes (coagulase, hyaluronidase, streptokinase) | *Streptococcus pyogenes* spreads in cellulitis |
| Damage | Exotoxins, endotoxin, cell destruction, immune reaction | Tetanus toxin, cholera toxin, septic shock |
| Exit | Secretions, faeces, blood, lesions | Cough in TB, faeces in typhoid |

## 3.2 Gram-positive cocci

| Organism | Characteristics | Source and transmission | Diseases | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ***Staphylococcus aureus*** | Cocci in grape-like clusters; non-motile; golden colonies; coagulase and catalase positive; tolerates salt and drying | Nose and skin of carriers (many people); hands of staff; contact, fomites | Boils, carbuncles, abscess, wound and surgical site infection, impetigo, osteomyelitis, pneumonia, septicaemia, food poisoning (toxin in food), toxic shock syndrome. **MRSA** = methicillin-resistant strains, a major hospital pathogen | Gram stain of pus, culture on blood agar (beta haemolysis), coagulase test, sensitivity test |
| *Staphylococcus epidermidis* | Coagulase negative; normal skin flora | Patient's own skin | Infections of IV catheters, prosthetic valves and joints | Culture of blood (more than one bottle positive) |
| ***Streptococcus pyogenes*** (group A, beta-haemolytic) | Cocci in chains; clear (beta) haemolysis on blood agar | Throat and skin; droplets, contact | Sore throat (pharyngitis), tonsillitis, scarlet fever, impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas, puerperal sepsis. Late non-suppurative complications: **rheumatic fever** and **acute glomerulonephritis** | Throat swab culture; **ASO** titre for past infection |
| ***Streptococcus pneumoniae*** (pneumococcus) | Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci; capsule; alpha (green) haemolysis | Upper respiratory tract; droplets | Lobar pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis | Sputum Gram stain and culture; urinary antigen; preventable by pneumococcal vaccine |
| *Streptococcus viridans* group | Alpha-haemolytic; mouth flora | Mouth (after dental procedures) | Infective endocarditis on damaged valves | Blood culture |
| *Enterococcus* | Gram-positive cocci in pairs/short chains; gut flora; hardy | Gut; hands, equipment | Urinary tract infection, wound infection, endocarditis; vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) in hospitals | Culture |

## 3.3 Gram-negative cocci

| Organism | Characteristics | Transmission | Diseases | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ***Neisseria meningitidis*** (meningococcus) | Kidney-shaped Gram-negative diplococci, often inside pus cells; capsule | Droplets from nasopharyngeal carriers; crowding | Meningococcal meningitis, septicaemia with purpuric rash | CSF Gram stain and culture on chocolate agar in CO2; antigen tests |
| ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae*** (gonococcus) | Kidney-shaped diplococci inside pus cells | Sexual contact; mother to baby during birth | Gonorrhoea (urethritis, cervicitis), pelvic inflammatory disease, **ophthalmia neonatorum** | Gram stain of urethral pus; culture on selective media |

## 3.4 Gram-positive bacilli

| Organism | Characteristics | Source and transmission | Disease | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ***Corynebacterium diphtheriae*** | Club-shaped rods in "Chinese letter" pattern; metachromatic granules | Droplets from cases and carriers | **Diphtheria**: grey pseudomembrane in throat that can block the airway; exotoxin damages heart and nerves | Throat swab; Albert's stain; culture on Loeffler's serum slope and tellurite medium; toxin test |
| ***Clostridium tetani*** | Anaerobic, spore-forming; "drumstick" (terminal round spore) | Spores in soil, dust, animal dung; enter through wounds, the umbilical stump (unclean cord care) | **Tetanus**: exotoxin causes muscle spasm, lockjaw, risus sardonicus; neonatal tetanus | Mainly clinical diagnosis; prevented by tetanus toxoid (Td) and clean delivery |
| *Clostridium perfringens* | Anaerobic, spore-bearing, capsulate, non-motile | Soil, gut; deep crushed wounds | **Gas gangrene** (spreading muscle necrosis with gas); food poisoning | Gram stain of exudate; anaerobic culture |
| *Clostridium botulinum* | Anaerobic, spore-bearing | Toxin in badly preserved canned food | Botulism — paralysis | Toxin detection |
| ***Clostridioides difficile*** | Anaerobic, spore-bearing | Hospital environment, hands; spores survive alcohol rub | Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis | Toxin test of stool; **soap-and-water hand washing** needed |
| *Bacillus anthracis* | Large rods in chains ("bamboo stick"); spores; capsule | Animals and their products (hides, wool) | Anthrax (skin, lung, gut) | Smear and culture |
| ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis*** | Slender acid-fast rods; aerobic; slow-growing; resists drying | Airborne droplet nuclei from open pulmonary cases; rarely unpasteurised milk (*M. bovis*) | **Tuberculosis** — lungs and any organ | Sputum ZN smear, cartridge-based molecular test (also detects rifampicin resistance), culture on Lowenstein–Jensen or liquid media (weeks), chest X-ray; Mantoux test (infection, not disease) |
| ***Mycobacterium leprae*** | Acid-fast; cannot be grown in artificial media | Prolonged close contact, nasal discharge of untreated cases | **Leprosy**: skin patches with loss of sensation, nerve thickening | Slit-skin smear (ZN with 5% H2SO4); clinical diagnosis |

## 3.5 Gram-negative bacilli

| Organism | Characteristics | Source and transmission | Diseases | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ***Escherichia coli*** | Motile; lactose fermenter (pink on MacConkey); normal gut flora | Own gut flora; contaminated food and water | **Urinary tract infection** (most common cause), diarrhoea (travellers' and infant), neonatal meningitis, wound infection, septicaemia | Urine culture with colony count; stool culture |
| ***Klebsiella pneumoniae*** | Non-motile; large mucoid capsule; lactose fermenter | Gut and respiratory tract; hospital environment, hands | Pneumonia, UTI, neonatal sepsis; many hospital strains are multidrug resistant (ESBL, carbapenem-resistant) | Culture and sensitivity |
| ***Salmonella* Typhi and Paratyphi** | Motile; non-lactose fermenter | Faeco-oral — food and water contaminated by patients or carriers (gall bladder carriers); flies | **Enteric (typhoid) fever** — step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots; complications: intestinal perforation and bleeding | **Blood culture** (best in the first week), stool and urine culture (later weeks), **Widal test** (antibodies, after the first week; interpret with care) |
| Other *Salmonella* | — | Poultry, eggs, meat | Food poisoning (gastroenteritis) | Stool culture |
| ***Shigella*** | Non-motile; non-lactose fermenter | Faeco-oral; very small infective dose; flies, fingers | **Bacillary dysentery** — frequent small stools with blood and mucus | Stool culture |
| ***Vibrio cholerae*** | Curved comma-shaped; very actively motile (darting); grows in alkaline media | Contaminated water and food | **Cholera** — profuse "rice-water" stools, severe dehydration | Hanging drop; stool culture in alkaline peptone water and TCBS agar; rapid tests |
| ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa*** | Motile; non-fermenter; blue-green pigment, grape-like smell; survives in moist places and some disinfectants | Sinks, humidifiers, wet equipment, hands | Burns and wound infection, ventilator-associated pneumonia, UTI with catheters; naturally resistant to many antibiotics | Culture |
| *Proteus* | Swarming motility; urease positive | Gut | UTI, kidney stones | Culture |
| *Acinetobacter baumannii* | Coccobacilli; survives long on dry surfaces | ICU environment, equipment, hands | Ventilator pneumonia, bloodstream and wound infections; often extensively drug-resistant | Culture |
| *Haemophilus influenzae* | Small coccobacilli; needs factors in blood (grows on chocolate agar) | Droplets | Meningitis and pneumonia in young children (type b, prevented by Hib in the pentavalent vaccine), epiglottitis | CSF culture |
| *Bordetella pertussis* | Small coccobacilli | Droplets | Whooping cough | Nasopharyngeal swab culture, PCR |
| *Helicobacter pylori* | Curved, microaerophilic | Faeco-oral / oral–oral | Gastritis, peptic ulcer | Urea breath test, biopsy |

**Spirochaetes and special bacteria**

| Organism | Transmission | Disease | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Treponema pallidum* | Sexual; mother to fetus | **Syphilis** (primary chancre → secondary rash → tertiary), congenital syphilis | Dark-ground microscopy of chancre fluid; **VDRL/RPR** (screening), TPHA (confirmatory) |
| *Leptospira* | Contact with water or soil contaminated by urine of rats and cattle (floods, paddy fields) | **Leptospirosis** — fever, jaundice, kidney failure (Weil's disease) | Serology (IgM ELISA, microscopic agglutination test) |
| *Orientia tsutsugamushi* (rickettsia) | Bite of larval mite (chigger) | **Scrub typhus** — fever with an eschar | Serology (IgM ELISA), Weil–Felix test (older) |
| *Chlamydia trachomatis* | Contact (eye), sexual | Trachoma, genital infection, neonatal conjunctivitis | Antigen tests, PCR |
| *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* | Droplets | Atypical pneumonia | Serology, PCR |

## 3.6 Viruses

**Characteristics**

- Smallest infectious agents (about 20–300 nm); seen only with the electron microscope.
- Contain **only one kind of nucleic acid** — DNA or RNA — in a protein coat (**capsid**); some have an outer lipid **envelope** (HIV, influenza, hepatitis B). Enveloped viruses are more easily destroyed by alcohol, soap and detergents.
- **Obligate intracellular parasites** — multiply only inside living cells using the host cell's machinery.
- Not affected by antibacterial antibiotics; some are treated with antiviral drugs; many are prevented by vaccines.

**Multiplication (replication) of a virus**

```text
 1 Adsorption (attachment to receptor) → 2 Penetration → 3 Uncoating
 → 4 Synthesis of viral nucleic acid and proteins → 5 Assembly (maturation)
 → 6 Release (by cell lysis or budding)
```

**Cultivation**: in laboratory animals, embryonated hen's eggs, and cell (tissue) cultures. **Diagnosis**: antigen detection (rapid tests, ELISA), antibody detection (IgM = recent infection), nucleic acid tests (PCR, RT-PCR), electron microscopy, virus isolation.

**Important viral diseases**

| Route | Virus — disease | Key points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory (droplet/airborne) | Influenza; SARS-CoV-2 — COVID-19; measles; mumps; rubella; varicella-zoster (chickenpox, shingles) | Measles and varicella spread by air (airborne precautions); rubella in early pregnancy causes congenital defects |
| Faeco-oral | Poliovirus — poliomyelitis; hepatitis A and E — infective hepatitis; rotavirus — infant diarrhoea | Hepatitis E is dangerous in pregnancy; polio and rotavirus prevented by vaccines in the national schedule |
| Blood, sexual, mother to child | **HIV** — AIDS; **hepatitis B, C** (and D with B) | Main risk to nurses through needle-stick injury; hepatitis B vaccine protects |
| Vector-borne | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika (*Aedes*); Japanese encephalitis (*Culex*); Kyasanur Forest disease (ticks) | Mosquito control and personal protection |
| Animal bite | Rabies (dog bite mainly) | Wound washing with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then post-exposure vaccination as advised; nearly always fatal once symptoms begin |
| Skin/mucosa contact | Herpes simplex; human papillomavirus (warts, cervical cancer) | HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer |

## 3.7 Fungi

**Characteristics**: eukaryotic; cell wall of chitin; no chlorophyll. Forms: **yeasts** (single round cells that bud — *Cryptococcus*), **yeast-like** (*Candida* forms buds and pseudohyphae), **moulds** (filaments called hyphae forming a mycelium — *Aspergillus*, *Mucor*, dermatophytes), **dimorphic** (mould in soil at room temperature, yeast in the body at 37 °C — *Histoplasma*).

**Classification of mycoses (fungal infections)**

| Type | Where | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Superficial** | Outermost layer of skin, hair shaft; little or no reaction | Pityriasis versicolor (*Malassezia* — scaly patches), black piedra, tinea nigra |
| Cutaneous (often taught with superficial) | Skin, hair and nails (keratin) | **Dermatophytes** (*Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, *Epidermophyton*) — ringworm: tinea capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium; cutaneous candidiasis |
| Subcutaneous | Below the skin after a thorn prick or injury | Mycetoma (Madura foot), sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis |
| **Deep (systemic)** | Internal organs; spread from lungs | Histoplasmosis, blastomycosis; cryptococcal meningitis |
| Opportunistic | In people with low immunity (diabetes, cancer, AIDS, steroids, ICU) | Candidiasis (oral thrush, vaginitis, candidaemia from central lines), aspergillosis, **mucormycosis** (seen after COVID-19 with uncontrolled diabetes and steroid use) |

**Identification**: KOH mount of skin, hair, nail scrapings; Gram stain (Candida = large Gram-positive budding cells); India ink for *Cryptococcus* in CSF; culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar; LPCB mount of the growth; antigen tests.

Nursing: keep skin folds dry; oral care in sick and immunocompromised patients; care of central lines; avoid sharing combs and towels (ringworm).

## 3.8 Parasites

A **parasite** lives on or in a host and gets food from it. **Protozoa** are single-celled; **helminths** are worms.

| Parasite | Disease | Transmission | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Entamoeba histolytica* | Amoebic dysentery; amoebic liver abscess | Faeco-oral — cysts in water and food | Fresh stool for trophozoites (with ingested red cells) and cysts; serology for liver abscess |
| *Giardia lamblia* | Diarrhoea, malabsorption | Faeco-oral cysts | Stool microscopy |
| ***Plasmodium*** (*vivax*, *falciparum*, *malariae*, *ovale*) | **Malaria** — cyclical fever with chills; *P. falciparum* causes severe/cerebral malaria | Bite of infected female ***Anopheles*** mosquito; also blood transfusion, mother to fetus | **Peripheral blood smear** (thick for detection, thin for species); rapid diagnostic tests (antigen) |
| *Leishmania donovani* | **Kala-azar** (visceral leishmaniasis) — fever, big spleen, darkening of skin | Sandfly (*Phlebotomus*) | Bone marrow or spleen aspirate; rapid antibody test |
| *Trichomonas vaginalis* | Vaginitis with frothy discharge | Sexual | Wet mount |
| *Toxoplasma gondii* | Congenital infection; brain infection in AIDS | Cat faeces, undercooked meat | Serology |
| ***Ascaris lumbricoides*** (roundworm) | Intestinal obstruction, malnutrition | Eggs in soil-contaminated food, unwashed hands | Eggs in stool |
| **Hookworm** (*Ancylostoma duodenale*, *Necator americanus*) | **Iron-deficiency anaemia** | Larvae in soil **penetrate bare skin** of feet | Eggs in stool |
| *Enterobius vermicularis* (pinworm) | Itching around the anus at night, especially children | Eggs on fingers, bedding; self-reinfection | Cellophane (adhesive) tape test of perianal skin in the morning |
| *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm) | Intestinal taeniasis; **neurocysticercosis** (seizures) when eggs are swallowed | Undercooked pork; eggs via faeco-oral route | Stool, CT/MRI brain, serology |
| *Echinococcus granulosus* | Hydatid cyst (liver, lung) | Eggs from dog faeces | Imaging, serology |
| *Wuchereria bancrofti* | **Lymphatic filariasis** — lymphoedema, elephantiasis, hydrocele | Bite of ***Culex*** mosquito | **Night blood smear** (microfilariae circulate at night), antigen card test |

Prevention of intestinal parasites: safe drinking water, sanitary latrines, hand washing, wearing footwear, cooking meat well, periodic deworming as per the national programme.

## 3.9 Rodents and vectors

A **vector** is an arthropod (insect or tick) that carries an infection from one host to another. Transmission is **mechanical** (carried on legs or body, e.g. housefly) or **biological** (the organism multiplies or develops inside the vector, e.g. malaria in *Anopheles*).

| Vector | Diseases |
| --- | --- |
| *Anopheles* mosquito (female) | Malaria |
| *Aedes aegypti* mosquito (day-biting, breeds in clean stored water, coolers, tyres) | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever |
| *Culex* mosquito (breeds in dirty water, drains) | Lymphatic filariasis (bancroftian), Japanese encephalitis |
| *Mansonia* mosquito | Brugian filariasis |
| Sandfly | Kala-azar |
| Housefly (mechanical) | Typhoid, cholera, dysentery, diarrhoea, trachoma, intestinal worms |
| Human louse | Epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, trench fever |
| Rat flea (*Xenopsylla cheopis*) | Plague, endemic (murine) typhus |
| Mites | Scrub typhus (larval mite), scabies (itch mite) |
| Hard ticks | Kyasanur Forest disease, tick typhus |
| Cockroach (mechanical) | Gut infections in hospital kitchens and wards |

**Rodents (rats, mice)** act as reservoirs: **plague** (via rat fleas), **leptospirosis** (urine), murine typhus, salmonellosis (droppings in food), rat-bite fever, and they damage stores and wiring.

**Control**

1. **Environmental**: remove breeding sites — no stagnant water, cover water tanks, empty coolers weekly, clear drains, proper garbage disposal, rodent-proof buildings and food stores.
2. **Personal protection**: mosquito nets (long-lasting insecticidal nets), repellents, full sleeves, screens.
3. **Chemical**: insecticide spraying (indoor residual spraying, fogging during outbreaks), larvicides; rodenticides and traps for rats.
4. **Biological**: larva-eating fish (*Gambusia*, guppy) in ponds and wells.
5. Health education and community participation.

In hospitals, pest control by an approved agency, screened windows, closed bins and no food left in wards keep vectors and rodents out.

## 3.10 Application and implication in nursing

- Match precautions to the route: **airborne** for TB, measles, chickenpox; **droplet** for influenza, diphtheria, meningococcus, pertussis; **contact** for MRSA, *C. difficile*, scabies, wound infections; **standard** for all, including HIV and hepatitis B (blood-borne).
- Collect the right specimen at the right time: blood culture in the first week of typhoid, night blood for filaria, smear during fever for malaria, fresh warm stool for amoebae, early-morning sputum for TB.
- Educate patients and families on safe water, food hygiene, mosquito control and completing treatment.
- Report notifiable diseases as per local rules (e.g. cholera, plague, diphtheria) and suspected outbreaks to the infection control team.
- Use soap and water (not alcohol rub) for *C. difficile* and norovirus.

## Remember

- *S. aureus*: clusters, coagulase positive, boils and wound infection; MRSA in hospitals.
- *S. pyogenes*: chains, beta haemolysis; rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis follow.
- Gram-negative diplococci: meningococcus (meningitis), gonococcus (gonorrhoea, ophthalmia neonatorum).
- *C. tetani*: drumstick spore, soil, wounds, cord; prevented by tetanus toxoid.
- *M. tuberculosis*: acid-fast, airborne, LJ medium, slow growth.
- *E. coli* is the commonest cause of UTI; typhoid — blood culture first week, Widal after.
- Cholera: comma-shaped, darting motility, rice-water stools, TCBS.
- Viruses: one nucleic acid, obligate intracellular, not killed by antibacterial antibiotics.
- Fungi: superficial (pityriasis versicolor), cutaneous (ringworm), deep (histoplasmosis), opportunistic (candida, aspergillus, mucor). KOH mount, SDA culture.
- *Anopheles* → malaria; *Aedes* → dengue, chikungunya; *Culex* → filaria, JE; sandfly → kala-azar; rat flea → plague; rat urine → leptospirosis; chigger → scrub typhus.
- Hookworm enters through bare feet and causes anaemia; pinworm — tape test.

# Unit 4: Immunity, hypersensitivity, serology and immunization

Section A (Applied Microbiology), INC Unit IV: immunity (types and classification), antigen–antibody reaction, hypersensitivity, serological tests, immunoglobulins, vaccines, storage and cold chain, and the immunization schedule.

## 4.1 Immunity: definition and classification

**Immunity** is the resistance of the body to infection and to foreign substances. The **immune system** recognises "self" from "non-self" and removes what is foreign.

```text
                         IMMUNITY
            ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
     INNATE (natural, non-specific)    ACQUIRED (adaptive, specific)
     – present from birth              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
     – species, racial, individual   ACTIVE               PASSIVE
                                     (own antibodies)     (ready-made antibodies)
                                   ┌──────┴─────┐       ┌──────┴───────┐
                                Natural    Artificial  Natural     Artificial
                                (infection) (vaccine)  (mother →   (immunoglobulin,
                                                        baby)       antiserum)
```

### Innate (non-specific) immunity

Present from birth; acts quickly; the same against every organism; no memory.

| Line of defence | Components |
| --- | --- |
| First line — barriers | Intact skin; mucous membranes with mucus; cilia of respiratory tract; cough and sneeze reflexes; tears and saliva (lysozyme); acid of the stomach; acid pH of vagina; flushing by urine; normal flora |
| Second line — internal non-specific defences | **Phagocytes** (neutrophils, macrophages); **natural killer (NK) cells**; **complement** proteins; **interferons** (block virus spread); **inflammation** (redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function); **fever** |

### Acquired (adaptive, specific) immunity

Develops after exposure to an antigen; specific to that antigen; has **memory**, so the second response is faster and stronger.

| Feature | Active immunity | Passive immunity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Antibodies made by | The person's own body | Another person or animal; given ready-made |
| Onset | Slow (days to weeks; a lag period) | Immediate |
| Duration | Long (months to years, often life-long) | Short (weeks to a few months) |
| Memory | Yes; booster responses | No |
| Natural examples | Recovery from measles or chickenpox | Maternal IgG across the placenta; IgA in colostrum and breast milk |
| Artificial examples | Vaccines (BCG, measles, tetanus toxoid) | Immunoglobulins and antisera: rabies immunoglobulin, hepatitis B immunoglobulin, anti-snake venom, anti-tetanus immunoglobulin |
| Use | Prevention | Immediate protection after exposure, or when there is no time to build immunity |

**Humoral versus cell-mediated immunity**

| | Humoral | Cell-mediated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cells | B lymphocytes → plasma cells | T lymphocytes (helper CD4, cytotoxic CD8) |
| Product | Antibodies in blood and secretions | Activated cells; cytokines |
| Main targets | Bacteria and toxins in body fluids, viruses before they enter cells | Viruses inside cells, TB, fungi, cancer cells, grafts |
| Example | Antitoxin neutralises tetanus toxin | Mantoux reaction; graft rejection |

**Primary and secondary response**: on first exposure antibodies appear after a lag of about one to two weeks, mainly **IgM**, in low amounts. On second exposure (or a booster) the response is quicker, larger and mainly **IgG** — the basis of booster doses.

## 4.2 Antigen and antibody

- **Antigen**: any substance that the body recognises as foreign and that provokes a specific immune response (proteins, polysaccharides; parts of microbes, toxins, pollen, transplanted tissue). The small part that binds to an antibody is the **epitope** (antigenic determinant). A **hapten** is a small molecule that becomes antigenic only when joined to a protein carrier (e.g. some drugs such as penicillin).
- **Antibody (immunoglobulin, Ig)**: a protein (gamma globulin) made by plasma cells in response to an antigen, which combines specifically with it.

**Antigen–antibody reaction**: the antibody binds the antigen like a lock and key; the binding is specific, reversible and needs the right proportion of both. Results: neutralisation of toxins and viruses, clumping (agglutination), precipitation, opsonisation (coating that helps phagocytosis), and activation of complement that bursts the cell.

## 4.3 Immunoglobulins: structure, types and properties

```text
        antigen-binding sites (variable regions)
           \  /             \  /
            \/               \/
            ||  light chain  ||
            ||   (L)         ||
             \\             //
              \\  hinge    //   ← disulphide bonds join chains
               ||         ||
               || heavy   ||
               || chains  ||
               ||   (H)   ||
              Fc (constant) region — binds cells and complement
```

- Basic unit: **four polypeptide chains** — two identical **heavy** and two identical **light** chains, held by disulphide bonds, in a Y shape.
- **Fab** (fragment antigen-binding) — the two arms; the tips (variable regions) bind antigen.
- **Fc** (fragment crystallisable) — the stem; decides what the antibody does (crossing the placenta, binding phagocytes, mast cells, complement).
- Five classes, named by the heavy chain: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE.

| Class | Structure | Approximate share of serum Ig | Key properties |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **IgG** | Monomer | Largest (about 75–80%) | Main antibody of the secondary response; **only one that crosses the placenta** (protects the newborn); neutralises toxins; longest half-life (about 3 weeks) |
| **IgA** | Monomer in serum; **dimer** in secretions (secretory IgA) | About 10–15% | Protects mucous surfaces (gut, respiratory, urinary); present in **colostrum**, breast milk, saliva, tears |
| **IgM** | **Pentamer** — the largest | About 5–10% | **First antibody** made in an infection; its presence means **recent infection** (e.g. IgM anti-HAV, dengue IgM); good at agglutination and complement activation; does not cross placenta, so IgM in a newborn means infection of the baby |
| **IgD** | Monomer | Less than 1% | On the surface of B cells as an antigen receptor |
| **IgE** | Monomer | Smallest amount | Binds mast cells and basophils; causes **allergy and anaphylaxis** (type I hypersensitivity); defence against worms |

Memory aid: **IgM = first ("M" for "make first"), IgG = goes across the placenta, IgA = in secretions, IgE = allergy, IgD = B-cell receptor.**

## 4.4 Hypersensitivity reactions

**Hypersensitivity** is an exaggerated or inappropriate immune response that damages the body. Gell and Coombs classification:

| Type | Mechanism | Onset | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **I — Immediate (anaphylactic)** | Allergen binds IgE on mast cells → release of histamine and other mediators | Minutes | **Anaphylaxis** (to drugs, insect stings, foods), asthma, hay fever, urticaria |
| **II — Cytotoxic** | IgG or IgM against antigens on cell surfaces → cell destruction with complement | Minutes to hours | **Mismatched blood transfusion reaction**, haemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh incompatibility), autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, drug-induced cytopenias |
| **III — Immune complex** | Antigen–antibody complexes deposit in vessel walls, kidneys, joints → inflammation | Hours to days | Serum sickness, Arthus reaction, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, systemic lupus erythematosus |
| **IV — Delayed (cell-mediated)** | Sensitised T cells release cytokines | 24–72 hours | **Mantoux (tuberculin) test**, contact dermatitis (nickel, latex, plants), graft rejection |

**Nursing in hypersensitivity**

- Take an allergy history before giving any drug, blood or vaccine; record allergies on the chart and wristband.
- Observe for 15–30 minutes after an injection or vaccine as per protocol; keep an **anaphylaxis kit** ready.
- Early signs of anaphylaxis: itching, flushing, urticaria, swelling of lips and face, wheeze, hoarseness, low blood pressure. Stop the drug or infusion, call for help, keep the airway open, lay the patient flat with legs raised (sitting up if breathless), give oxygen and emergency drugs as prescribed by protocol, and monitor.
- In a transfusion reaction: stop the transfusion at once, keep the line open with saline, inform the doctor and blood bank, return the bag and set, collect blood and urine samples.
- Rh-negative mothers receive anti-D immunoglobulin as prescribed to prevent Rh sensitisation.
- Latex allergy: use latex-free gloves and equipment.

## 4.5 Serological tests

**Serology** is the study of antigen–antibody reactions in serum, used to diagnose infection (by finding antibody or antigen), group blood and test for immunity.

| Reaction | Principle | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Agglutination** | Antibody clumps particulate antigens (cells, bacteria, latex beads) | **Widal test** (typhoid), blood grouping and cross-matching, latex agglutination (CRP, RA factor, ASO), Weil–Felix test (rickettsiae) |
| **Precipitation / flocculation** | Antibody combines with soluble antigen to form a visible precipitate | **VDRL** and RPR (syphilis), immunodiffusion |
| Complement fixation | Antigen–antibody complex uses up complement | Older tests for some viral infections |
| Neutralisation | Antibody blocks a toxin or virus | Tests of toxins and viral antibodies |
| **ELISA** (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) | Enzyme-labelled antibody gives a colour change | HIV antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), dengue NS1 antigen and IgM |
| Immunofluorescence | Fluorescent-labelled antibody seen under UV microscope | Some viral and autoimmune tests |
| **Rapid card tests (immunochromatography)** | Antigen or antibody moves along a strip and forms a coloured line | Malaria antigen RDT, HIV rapid test, pregnancy test, COVID-19 antigen test |
| Western blot | Antibodies to separated proteins | Confirmatory test in some infections |
| Chemiluminescence (CLIA) | Light-producing label; automated | Hormone and infection markers in large labs |

Interpreting serology: a **rising titre** (fourfold rise between two samples 10–14 days apart) or **IgM** shows current infection; IgG alone may mean past infection or vaccination. The **window period** is the time after infection before tests turn positive (important in HIV testing and blood donation).

Nursing: collect blood in a plain (red-top) tube for serum, avoid haemolysis, label correctly, note vaccination history and date of onset of illness.

## 4.6 Vaccines: types and classification

A **vaccine** is a preparation of a killed or weakened organism, its toxin made harmless, or a part of it, that produces active immunity without causing the disease.

| Type | What it contains | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Live attenuated** | Living organisms weakened so they cannot cause disease | **BCG**, **OPV** (oral polio), **measles–rubella (MR)**, rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever, live JE vaccine | Usually one or two doses give long immunity; generally avoided in pregnancy and in people with weak immunity; most are heat-sensitive |
| **Killed (inactivated)** | Whole organisms killed by heat or chemicals | **IPV** (injectable polio), rabies cell-culture vaccine, hepatitis A, whole-cell pertussis (in DPT/pentavalent) | Several doses and boosters needed; safe in low immunity |
| **Toxoid** | Bacterial exotoxin made harmless (formaldehyde) but still antigenic | **Tetanus toxoid**, diphtheria toxoid (in DPT, Td) | Protects against the toxin |
| **Subunit / recombinant** | Purified part of the organism, often made by genetic engineering | **Hepatitis B** vaccine (HBsAg), HPV vaccine, acellular pertussis | Very safe |
| **Conjugate** | Polysaccharide joined to a protein carrier so infants respond well | **Hib** (in pentavalent), **pneumococcal conjugate (PCV)** | Infants respond poorly to plain polysaccharide |
| Newer platforms | mRNA, viral vector, protein subunit | COVID-19 vaccines | — |
| Combination | Several antigens in one injection | **Pentavalent** (DPT + hepatitis B + Hib), MR | Fewer injections |

**Adjuvants** (such as aluminium salts) in some vaccines boost the immune response; these "adsorbed" vaccines are damaged by freezing.

## 4.7 Storage, handling and the cold chain

The **cold chain** is the system of people, equipment and procedures that keeps vaccines at the recommended temperature from the manufacturer to the point of use. Heat and (for some) freezing destroy potency, and damage cannot be seen or reversed.

```text
 Manufacturer → Government Medical Store Depot → State store → Regional/District store
   → PHC / CHC (ice-lined refrigerator) → Sub-centre / session site (vaccine carrier)
   → Child
```

| Equipment | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Walk-in coolers and freezers | Large state and regional stores |
| **Ice-lined refrigerator (ILR)** | Main storage at district and PHC levels; keeps +2 °C to +8 °C even with some power cuts |
| **Deep freezer** | Freezing ice packs (and, at higher levels, storing OPV frozen) |
| Cold box | Transporting and storing for a few days during campaigns or power failure |
| **Vaccine carrier with 4 conditioned ice packs** | Taking vaccines to the session site for the day |
| Thermometers, temperature logbooks, data loggers; eVIN (electronic vaccine stock and temperature monitoring) | Monitoring |

**Rules of storage**

- Most vaccines at **+2 °C to +8 °C**. Keep a thermometer in the ILR and record the temperature twice daily.
- **Freeze-sensitive vaccines** (never freeze): hepatitis B, pentavalent, DPT, Td, IPV, PCV, and others with adjuvants. Keep them away from the ILR floor and the freezing surfaces. If freezing is suspected, the **shake test** shows whether the vaccine was frozen (frozen vaccine settles faster with flakes).
- **Heat-sensitive vaccines**: OPV, measles–rubella, BCG, rotavirus — keep in the coldest permitted place, protect from heat and sunlight.
- **Vaccine vial monitor (VVM)**: a heat-sensitive square inside a circle on the label. If the inner square is lighter than the outer circle the vaccine can be used (if not expired). If the square matches or is darker than the circle (discard point), do not use.
- Diluents are kept cold before reconstitution and only the diluent supplied with that vaccine is used.
- Reconstituted vaccines (BCG, measles–rubella, JE) are used within 4 hours or by the end of the session, whichever is earlier, then discarded. Under the **open vial policy**, opened multi-dose vials of some liquid vaccines (such as OPV, DPT, Td, hepatitis B, pentavalent and IPV) may be used in later sessions for up to 4 weeks if conditions are met (not expired, VVM usable, cold chain maintained, no contamination, date of opening written). Check the current national guidelines for the exact list.
- Conditioned ice packs: frozen packs are kept out until the ice starts to melt (water sloshes) before putting them in carriers, so freeze-sensitive vaccines are not frozen.
- Use the "**Earliest Expiry First Out**" principle; never keep food or drinks in the vaccine refrigerator.

**Adverse events following immunization (AEFI)**: minor (pain, swelling, fever) and serious (anaphylaxis, seizures, death, hospitalisation). Observe for 30 minutes after vaccination, report serious AEFI through the national surveillance system, and keep an AEFI kit at every session.

## 4.8 Immunization schedule

The **National Immunization Schedule (NIS)** of the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) is set by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The table below follows the NIS as published on the National Health Mission website. The schedule is updated from time to time, so check the current version on the MoHFW / NHM site before an exam or a clinical posting.

| Age | Vaccines |
| --- | --- |
| **Pregnant woman** | Td-1 early in pregnancy, Td-2 four weeks after Td-1; a single Td booster if she received two doses in a pregnancy within the last 3 years |
| **Birth** | BCG, OPV-0 (zero dose), hepatitis B birth dose |
| **6 weeks** | OPV-1, Pentavalent-1, Rotavirus (RVV)-1, fractional IPV (fIPV)-1, PCV-1 |
| **10 weeks** | OPV-2, Pentavalent-2, RVV-2 |
| **14 weeks** | OPV-3, Pentavalent-3, fIPV-2, RVV-3, PCV-2 |
| **9–12 months** | Measles–Rubella (MR)-1, JE-1 (in endemic districts), PCV booster |
| **16–24 months** | MR-2, JE-2 (endemic districts), DPT booster-1, OPV booster |
| **5–6 years** | DPT booster-2 |
| **10 years and 16 years** | Td |

Points to check in the current schedule: the NHM table showed PCV only in selected states when it was published, and PCV was later extended to the whole country; a third fIPV dose at 9 months has since been added. Vitamin A is given with some of these visits (it is a supplement, not a vaccine).

**Routes (learn with the schedule)**: BCG — intradermal, left upper arm; OPV — oral drops; RVV — oral; hepatitis B, pentavalent, PCV, DPT — intramuscular, anterolateral thigh in infants; fIPV — intradermal, right upper arm; MR — subcutaneous, right upper arm; Td in older children and pregnant women — intramuscular, upper arm. Follow the exact volume on the vaccine label and national guidelines.

**Vaccination for other diseases and groups**

- Rabies: post-exposure vaccination with or without rabies immunoglobulin depending on the category of bite.
- Tetanus: Td after injury as per immunization status.
- Hepatitis B for health care workers (see Unit 8).
- Typhoid, hepatitis A, influenza, varicella, HPV and COVID-19 vaccines are available. HPV vaccine is given to girls before they become sexually active to prevent cervical cancer; check whether it is part of the current national schedule in your state.
- Pulse polio campaigns give additional OPV to children under 5 years.

## 4.9 Role of the nurse in immunization

1. Plan sessions, list due beneficiaries, mobilise families.
2. Maintain the cold chain; check temperature, VVM and expiry before use.
3. Check contraindications and history of previous reactions; counsel the mother on what vaccine is given, expected minor reactions and next visit.
4. Use one new auto-disable syringe for every injection; follow injection safety and do not recap; put used syringes in a puncture-proof container (hub cutter).
5. Give the vaccine by the correct route and site; record in the MCP card and register / digital system.
6. Observe for 30 minutes; manage and report AEFI.
7. Track drop-outs; educate the community.

## Remember

- Innate = present at birth, non-specific, no memory. Acquired = specific, memory.
- Active natural = infection; active artificial = vaccine; passive natural = maternal antibodies; passive artificial = immunoglobulin/antiserum.
- IgG crosses the placenta and is the most abundant; IgM is first and pentameric; IgA in secretions and colostrum; IgE in allergy.
- Hypersensitivity: I anaphylaxis (IgE), II cytotoxic (transfusion reaction, Rh), III immune complex (serum sickness), IV delayed (Mantoux, contact dermatitis).
- Widal = agglutination; VDRL = flocculation; ELISA for HIV, HBsAg.
- Live vaccines: BCG, OPV, MR, rotavirus. Toxoid: tetanus, diphtheria. Recombinant: hepatitis B.
- Cold chain +2 °C to +8 °C; never freeze hepatitis B, pentavalent, DPT, Td, IPV; shake test detects freezing; VVM inner square lighter than circle = usable.
- Reconstituted BCG, MR, JE: use within 4 hours.
- Birth: BCG, OPV-0, Hep B. 6, 10, 14 weeks: OPV, Pentavalent, RVV (+ fIPV, PCV). 9 months: MR-1. 16–24 months: MR-2, DPT-B1, OPV booster. 5–6 years: DPT-B2. 10 and 16 years: Td.
